skills.name: Add and subtract integers, including subtracting a negative number
skills.mastery: The child adds and subtracts any two integers without a number line, knowing that subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its positive (5 - (-3) = 8) and adding a negative is the same as subtracting (4 + (-9) = -5), and gives the sign of the result correctly.

prerequisites.reason: Moving on the number line is what the rules shorten.
The gap across zero is a subtraction of a negative number.
Knowing which of two integers is larger decides the sign of a sum.

skills.name: Multiply and divide integers using the sign rules
skills.mastery: The child multiplies and divides integers, giving a positive answer when the signs are the same and a negative answer when they differ: (-4) x 6 = -24, (-4) x (-6) = 24, 18 / (-3) = -6, (-18) / (-3) = 6, and can explain the rule from a pattern of products.

prerequisites.reason: A repeated change (a fall of 3 m a month for 4 months) is a product of integers.

skills.name: Work out combined operations on integers in the right order
skills.mastery: The child works out an expression such as 7 - 3 x (-4) or -12 / 4 + 5 by doing multiplication and division before addition and subtraction, and left to right within the same rank, keeping the sign of every term: 7 - 3 x (-4) = 7 + 12 = 19.

prerequisites.reason: Every product and quotient needs its sign.
The order of operations with whole numbers.
The last steps are additions and subtractions of integers.

skills.name: Work out combined operations on integers with brackets, step by step
skills.mastery: The child works out an expression with brackets such as (-5 + 2) x (-4) - 18 / (-3) in steps: the bracket first, then each product and quotient with its sign, then the subtraction, changing minus a negative into plus: (-3) x (-4) = 12, 18 / (-3) = -6, 12 - (-6) = 18.

prerequisites.reason: Brackets come first, then the usual order.
The bracket often holds a sum of a negative and a positive.

skills.name: Use integers for balances, lifts and other changes in real life
skills.mastery: The child writes a real situation as integers (an overdraft as a negative balance, a basement floor as a negative floor), starts from the opening value, applies every change with its sign in order, and says what the final integer means in the story (still overdrawn, below the ground floor).

prerequisites.reason: Running balances with money in and out.
Each change is an addition or subtraction of an integer.
Writing a situation below zero as a negative integer.

skills.name: Find the difference between heights or temperatures above and below zero
skills.mastery: The child reads altitudes or temperatures from a table, picks the highest and the lowest, and finds the gap as highest minus lowest with signs: 450 - (-120) = 570 m, counting the part below zero and the part above it.

prerequisites.reason: The difference of two integers across zero.
Subtracting a negative number is adding.

skills.name: Work out the cube of a number by multiplication
skills.mastery: The child works out the cube of a whole number, a negative number, a decimal or a fraction by multiplying it by itself three times (2.5 x 2.5 x 2.5 = 15.625, (-4) x (-4) x (-4) = -64, (2/3) cubed = 8/27), and recognises the cube numbers up to 1,000.

prerequisites.reason: A square is the number multiplied by itself twice; a cube adds one more factor.
Multiplying decimals and counting decimal places.
The sign of the cube of a negative number.

skills.name: Find cubes of numbers from tables, including numbers outside 1 to 10
skills.mastery: The child reads the cube of a number such as 2.37 from the table (row 2.3, column 7) to 4 significant figures, and for a number outside 1 to 10 writes it as a number from the table times a power of 10 and multiplies the table value by that power cubed: 23.7 cubed = 2.37 cubed x 1,000.
question_forms: use the table for a larger number

prerequisites.reason: Reading a table of squares by row and column is the same skill.
Knowing what a cube is, to check a table value.
Table values are given to 4 significant figures.

skills.name: Find the cube root of a perfect cube by prime factors
skills.mastery: The child writes a perfect cube as a product of prime factors, puts the factors in groups of three equal primes, takes one prime from each group and multiplies them: 2,744 = (2x2x2)(7x7x7), so the cube root is 2 x 7 = 14.

prerequisites.reason: Writing a number as a product of primes.
The square root by factors uses pairs; the cube root uses groups of three.
Checking the root by cubing it.

skills.name: Find the smallest number that makes a number a perfect cube
skills.mastery: The child writes the number in prime factors, counts how many of each prime are short of a full group of three, and multiplies those missing primes: 72 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 needs one more 3, so the smallest multiplier is 3 and 216 = 6 cubed.

prerequisites.reason: The prime factors show what is missing.
Groups of three equal primes make a cube.

skills.name: Find cube roots from tables, including numbers outside 1 to 10
skills.mastery: The child reads the cube root of a number from 1 to 10 from the table, and for a larger number writes it as a number from the table times 1,000 or 1,000,000 so the cube root is the table value times 10 or 100: the cube root of 4,500 = cube root of 4.5 x 10.
question_forms: cube root of a large number

prerequisites.reason: Reading square roots from a table and moving the decimal point.
The table of cubes read the other way.
Writing a number as a number times a power of 10.

skills.name: Use cubes for the volume of cube-shaped tanks, cartons and boxes
skills.mastery: The child finds the volume of a cube from its edge (edge x edge x edge), changes m cubed to litres (1 m cubed = 1,000 litres), finds how many small cubes fill a large one (cubes along an edge, cubed), and explains that doubling the edge makes the volume 8 times as big.

prerequisites.reason: Changing cubic metres and cubic centimetres to litres.
Working out the cube of the edge.

skills.name: Use cube roots to find the edge of a cube from its volume
skills.mastery: The child finds the edge of a cube-shaped box or tank from its volume by taking the cube root (a box holding 3,375 cubic cm has edge 15 cm), by factors or a table, and checks by cubing the answer.

prerequisites.reason: The cube root of a perfect cube.
Volume of a cube is edge cubed.
The side of a square from its area is the same idea one dimension lower.

skills.name: Work out cubes and cube roots on a calculator and check the answer
skills.mastery: The child uses the cube key (x cubed or x^y with 3) and the cube root key on a calculator, puts a negative number in brackets, rounds the display to the accuracy asked (4 significant figures, 2 decimal places), and checks the answer against an estimate: the cube root of 50 is between 3 and 4 because 27 < 50 < 64.

prerequisites.reason: Squares on a calculator: the same keys one power lower.
Knowing the cube numbers to make an estimate.

sub_strands.design_notes: Official outcomes a to d are tested; e (use IT) and f (appreciate) are not questions. skills.name: Write numbers in index form and work out powers
skills.mastery: The child names the base and the index, writes a repeated product in index form (2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 2 to the power 5, 72 = 2 cubed x 3 squared) and works out a power by repeated multiplication (3 to the power 4 = 81), including growth that multiplies by the same number each step.

prerequisites.reason: A cube is a power with index 3.
Prime factors are written in index form.

skills.name: Multiply and divide powers of the same base by adding and subtracting indices
skills.mastery: The child shows from repeated factors that a to the m times a to the n is a to the (m + n) and a to the m divided by a to the n is a to the (m - n), keeps the base unchanged, and uses the laws to simplify and to work out values: 2 to the 5 x 2 to the 3 = 2 to the 8 = 256; 5 to the 7 divided by 5 to the 4 = 125.

prerequisites.reason: Writing powers as repeated factors is how the laws are seen.
Adding and subtracting indices, some of them negative.

skills.name: Use the zero index and the power of a power
skills.mastery: The child explains from the division law that any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1 (7 to the 3 divided by 7 to the 3 = 7 to the 0 = 1), and that a power of a power multiplies the indices: (2 cubed) squared = 2 to the 6.
question_forms: why is a to the 0 equal to 1
simplify the power of a power

prerequisites.reason: The zero index comes from the division law; a power of a power is repeated multiplication of powers.

skills.name: Simplify expressions and find unknown indices with several laws
skills.mastery: The child simplifies an expression such as (x cubed) to the 4 x x squared divided by x to the 5 in steps, one law at a time (x to the 12, x to the 14, x to the 9), works with numbers in front of the letters (2x cubed x 3x squared = 6x to the 5), and finds an unknown index by writing an equation for the indices.

prerequisites.reason: Multiplying indices for a power of a power.
Solving the equation for the unknown index.

skills.name: Relate powers of 10 to common logarithms
skills.mastery: The child writes a power of 10 such as 10,000 = 10 to the 4 and says its common logarithm is the index (log 10,000 = 4), continues the pattern below 1 (log 0.01 = -2) and knows log 1 = 0 and log 10 = 1.

skills.name: Use logarithms of powers of 10 to simplify sums and differences of logs
skills.mastery: The child adds logs of numbers whose product is a power of 10 (log 25 + log 40 = log 1,000 = 3) and subtracts them for a quotient, using log of a product = sum of logs because indices add when powers multiply, and uses given logs to find others (log 6 = log 2 + log 3).

prerequisites.reason: Knowing log of a power of 10.

skills.name: Use a logarithmic scale such as earthquake magnitude in real life
skills.mastery: The child reads a scale where each step of 1 multiplies the size by 10 (a tremor of magnitude 5 moves the ground 100 times as much as one of magnitude 3), writing each reading back as a power of 10 and dividing.

prerequisites.reason: Changing a logarithm back to a power of 10.

skills.name: Divide a quantity into proportional parts
skills.mastery: The child shares an amount in a ratio of two or three parts by adding the parts, finding the value of one part (amount divided by the total parts) and multiplying by each share: 36,000 shillings in the ratio 2:3:4 gives one part 4,000 and shares 8,000, 12,000 and 16,000, which add back to 36,000.

prerequisites.reason: Sharing in a ratio of two parts.
Finding one part from the total.

skills.name: Relate two ratios that share a term to make one ratio
skills.mastery: The child links a:b and b:c by making the shared term equal (multiply each ratio so the b values match, using the LCM), then writes a:b:c and uses it: cows:goats = 2:3 and goats:hens = 4:5 give cows:goats:hens = 8:12:15.

prerequisites.reason: The LCM makes the shared term equal.
Using a ratio of three parts.

skills.name: Solve compound proportion problems by the ratio method
skills.mastery: The child handles two changes at once (machines and hours, workers and shambas) by asking for each change whether it increases or decreases the answer and multiplying by the matching ratio, or by finding the amount for one unit of each first: 4 machines grind 1,200 kg in 6 hours, so 6 machines in 5 hours grind 1,200 x 6/4 x 5/6 = 1,500 kg.

prerequisites.reason: Direct and inverse proportion with one change.
Some of the changes act inversely.

skills.name: Recognise and use inverse proportion
skills.mastery: The child sees that more workers take fewer days (workers x days stays the same), checks a table by multiplying x and y in each row (inverse) or dividing (direct), and finds a missing value from the constant product: 6 workers take 10 days, so 60 worker-days, so 4 workers take 15 days.

prerequisites.reason: Solving a proportion with one change.

skills.name: Work out how long people or taps take when working together
skills.mastery: The child turns each time into the part of the job done in one unit of time (a tap that fills a tank in 4 hours fills 1/4 an hour), adds the parts for people working together, and turns the total back into a time; for a job finished by one person, takes the work done together from the whole and divides the rest by that person's rate.

prerequisites.reason: Adding the parts done in one hour.
Turning a rate back into a time.

skills.name: Work out times when one rate works against another (a pipe and a leak)
skills.mastery: The child finds the part filled in one hour by the pipe and the part emptied by the leak, subtracts the leak's part, and turns what is left back into a time: a pipe fills in 3 hours and a leak empties in 6 hours, so 1/3 - 1/6 = 1/6 a tank an hour, 6 hours.

prerequisites.reason: Rates as parts of a job per hour.

learning_experiences: discuss the use of tables such as football league tables, travel schedules, shopping lists and any other. Count the number of rows and columns in the table, which is a matrix.
arrange items in rows and columns and discuss how to represent a matrix.
organize objects in rows and columns and give the order of the matrix in terms of row and columns (row x column).
discuss and identify the position of each item or element in terms of row and column.
discuss and identify matrices that have equal number of rows and equal number of columns (same order) compatibility in addition and subtraction.
discuss and note what is represented the rows and what is represented by the columns from two or more matrices to carry out addition or subtraction.

sub_strands.design_notes: Official outcomes a to e are tested; f (reflect) is not a question. Matrices are new in Grade 9: a table of numbers in rows and columns (a), its order, rows first (b), the position of an element (c), when two matrices can be added or subtracted (d), and adding and subtracting them in real situations, including finding unknown elements (e). Multiplying matrices is not in the Grade 9 design. g9.mat.table-position was written under a but asks for an element by row and column, so it is filed under c. Two families build their options in code (add-why, compat-table) and are tied at family level. The existing families use the HOREB skills G11_MATRICES_INTRO and G11_MATRICES_OPS (named for the old Form 3 placement); a teacher should confirm the content suits Grade 9.

skills.name: Identify a matrix and write information as a matrix
skills.mastery: The child recognises a matrix as numbers arranged in rows and columns inside brackets, writes the numbers of a table (marks of learners in subjects, items sold by two shops on three days) as a matrix in the same order, and says what a row and a column stand for.
question_forms: write the table as a matrix

prerequisites.reason: Reading a table by rows and columns.

skills.name: Determine the order of a matrix
skills.mastery: The child gives the order of a matrix as the number of rows by the number of columns (a matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns has order 2 x 3), knows that 2 x 3 and 3 x 2 are different orders, and names row, column and square matrices.

prerequisites.reason: Knowing what rows and columns are.
An order is read in a fixed order, as coordinates are.

skills.name: Find the position of an element in a matrix
skills.mastery: The child finds the element in row i and column j by counting rows from the top and columns from the left (row first), and names the position of a given element: in a marks matrix, row 2 column 3 is the second learner's mark in the third subject.

prerequisites.reason: Reading a cell of a table.

skills.name: Decide whether two matrices can be added or subtracted
skills.mastery: The child compares the orders of two matrices and says they can be added or subtracted only when the orders are the same (same rows and same columns), not just the same number of elements, and picks the compatible pair from a list of orders.
question_forms: can A and B be added

prerequisites.reason: Matching elements must have partners in the same position.

skills.name: Add and subtract matrices, including in real-life situations
skills.mastery: The child adds or subtracts matching elements of two matrices of the same order, keeping the order of subtraction (first minus second) and the signs of negative elements, and uses it for real totals and differences: sales of two weeks added, stock left after sales subtracted.

prerequisites.reason: Only matrices of the same order are combined.

skills.name: Find unknown elements in a matrix equation
skills.mastery: The child matches the elements in the same position on each side of a matrix sum, writes a small equation for each unknown and solves it: [x 3; 2 y] + [4 1; 5 2] = [9 4; 7 6] gives x + 4 = 9, so x = 5, and y + 2 = 6, so y = 4.

prerequisites.reason: How the elements of a sum are made.

skills.name: Find the area of a regular pentagon or hexagon by splitting it into triangles from the centre
skills.mastery: The child joins the centre of a regular pentagon or hexagon to each corner, making 5 or 6 equal triangles with a centre angle of 360 / n degrees, finds one triangle as half base times height (the height from the centre to the middle of a side) and multiplies by the number of sides.
question_forms: why is the centre angle 72 degrees

prerequisites.reason: Splitting a shape into simpler parts.
Angles round the centre add to 360 degrees.

skills.name: Find the area of a pentagon or hexagon made of rectangles and triangles
skills.mastery: The child splits an irregular pentagon or hexagon (a plot, a gable wall) into a rectangle and triangles, finds each area (length x width; half base x height) and adds them, leaving no part out and counting no part twice.

prerequisites.reason: Area of a rectangle in context.

skills.name: Work out the surface area of triangular and rectangular prisms
skills.mastery: The child lists every face of the prism (two equal ends and one rectangle for each side of the end), finds each area, and adds them, leaving out faces that are open (a trough with no top): a triangular prism with ends 3, 4, 5 cm and length 10 cm has 2 x 6 + (3 + 4 + 5) x 10 = 132 square cm.

prerequisites.reason: Surface area of a triangular prism (Grade 8).

skills.name: Work out the surface area of pyramids, finding the slant height by Pythagoras
skills.mastery: The child finds the slant height of a square-based pyramid from the vertical height and half the base by Pythagoras, finds each triangular face as half base times slant height, and adds the base when it is there: base 6 cm, height 4 cm, slant 5 cm, so 4 x 15 + 36 = 96 square cm.

prerequisites.reason: The slant height is a hypotenuse.

skills.name: Calculate the area of a sector, and the angle from the area
skills.mastery: The child finds a sector as angle/360 of the circle (pi r squared), and works back from a sector's area to its angle by dividing by the whole circle and multiplying by 360: radius 7 cm, 90 degrees, 38.5 square cm.

prerequisites.reason: The area of the whole circle.

skills.name: Calculate the area of a segment of a circle
skills.mastery: The child finds a segment as the sector minus the triangle made by the two radii and the chord, for a right angle at the centre the triangle being half of r times r: radius 7 m, 90 degrees: 38.5 - 24.5 = 14 square m.
question_forms: area between the chord and the arc

skills.name: Work out the surface area of a cone
skills.mastery: The child finds the slant height l from the radius and the vertical height by Pythagoras, the curved surface as pi r l, and adds the base pi r squared for a closed cone: r = 3 cm, h = 4 cm, l = 5 cm, 15 pi + 9 pi = 24 pi square cm.

prerequisites.reason: A curved surface and circular faces.

skills.name: Calculate the surface area of a sphere and a hemisphere
skills.mastery: The child uses 4 pi r squared for a sphere, half of it for the curved part of a hemisphere, and adds the flat circle for a solid hemisphere (3 pi r squared), and uses the area for paint or plating: a tank of radius 7 m has 616 square m, so at 14 square m a litre it needs 44 litres.

prerequisites.reason: The sphere is 4 times the circle through its middle.

skills.name: Work out the volume of triangular and rectangular prisms and change it to litres
skills.mastery: The child finds the area of the end (a triangle, rectangle or trapezium) and multiplies by the length, then changes cubic cm to litres (divide by 1,000) or cubic m to litres (multiply by 1,000): a trough with triangular ends of base 40 cm and height 30 cm, 150 cm long, holds 90,000 cubic cm = 90 litres.
question_forms: area of the end times the length

prerequisites.reason: The end may be a trapezium.

skills.name: Calculate the volume of a pyramid and work back to its height
skills.mastery: The child finds a pyramid as one third of base area times height (one third of the prism on the same base and height), and works back to the height by multiplying the volume by 3 and dividing by the base area.

prerequisites.reason: The pyramid is a third of the prism.

skills.name: Work out the volume of a cone in real-life situations
skills.mastery: The child finds a cone as one third of pi r squared times h, using the radius (half the diameter), and uses the volume for loads and capacity: a heap of sand of radius 3.5 m and height 2 m is about 25.7 cubic m, so a lorry of 6 cubic m needs 5 trips.

prerequisites.reason: The cone is a third of the cylinder.
The one third, as for a pyramid.

skills.name: Determine the volume of a frustum
skills.mastery: The child finds the volume of a frustum (a bucket, a lampshade) as the whole cone minus the small cone cut off, each with its own radius and height, and changes it to litres; when the small cone is a scale copy, uses the cube of the scale factor.

skills.name: Calculate the volume of a sphere and a hemisphere
skills.mastery: The child uses four thirds pi r cubed for a sphere and two thirds pi r cubed for a hemisphere, uses the radius three times, and compares volumes of spheres by the cube of the radius: melting a sphere of radius 6 cm gives 8 spheres of radius 3 cm.

skills.name: Convert units of mass (mg, g, kg, tonnes) in real situations
skills.mastery: The child changes between milligrams, grams, kilograms and tonnes (1 tonne = 1,000 kg, 1 kg = 1,000 g, 1 g = 1,000 mg), puts masses in the same unit before adding or subtracting, and finds a load as the gross mass minus the empty lorry: 12.4 tonnes - 7,850 kg = 4.55 tonnes.
question_forms: mass of the load in tonnes

prerequisites.reason: Converting metric units by powers of 10.

skills.name: Relate mass and weight
skills.mastery: The child says mass (kg) is the amount of matter and stays the same everywhere, while weight (newtons) is the pull of gravity and changes from place to place, and works out weight = mass x g (a 50 kg sack weighs 500 N where g = 10 N/kg) and mass from weight.

prerequisites.reason: g is a rate: newtons for each kilogram.

skills.name: Determine mass, volume and density from each other
skills.mastery: The child uses density = mass / volume and its rearrangements (mass = density x volume, volume = mass / density), finds the volume of a regular solid first when needed, compares densities rather than masses, and reads density as the gradient of a mass-volume graph.

prerequisites.reason: Density is mass per unit of volume.
Density as the gradient of a graph.

skills.name: Convert density between g/cm cubed and kg/m cubed
skills.mastery: The child knows 1 g/cm cubed = 1,000 kg/m cubed (1,000 g in a kg and 1,000,000 cubic cm in a cubic m), so multiplies by 1,000 to go to kg/m cubed and divides by 1,000 to come back: 7.8 g/cm cubed = 7,800 kg/m cubed.
question_forms: write in kg per cubic m
write in g per cubic cm

skills.name: Use density to explain floating and sinking, and the volume of ice
skills.mastery: The child compares an object's density with the liquid's (less dense floats, denser sinks), not its mass or size alone, and uses density to find how much space a mass takes: 450 g of water (1 g/cm cubed) freezes to 500 cubic cm of ice (0.9 g/cm cubed).

skills.name: Apply density to displacement and mixtures
skills.mastery: The child finds the volume of an irregular stone by the rise in water level in a measuring cylinder, then its density; finds the mean density of a mixture as total mass over total volume (not the average of the densities); and uses a known density to find the mass of another piece.
question_forms: mass of a chip of the same stone

prerequisites.reason: A mean is a total divided by a total.

skills.name: Work out speed in km/h and m/s and change between them
skills.mastery: The child finds speed as distance over time with the time in hours for km/h (45 minutes = 0.75 h) or in seconds for m/s, and changes km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6 and m/s to km/h by multiplying by 3.6: 72 km/h = 20 m/s.

skills.name: Find when and where two vehicles moving towards each other meet
skills.mastery: The child adds the two speeds for vehicles moving towards each other (the gap closes at v1 + v2), finds the time to meet as the distance over that sum, and the meeting place from either vehicle's distance: 240 km apart at 50 and 70 km/h, they meet after 2 h, 100 km from the first town.

skills.name: Work out the average speed for a whole journey
skills.mastery: The child finds average speed as total distance over total time, counting rests and stops in the time, counting both ways of a there-and-back trip in the distance, and does not average the speeds of parts that take different times: 120 km at 60 km/h and 120 km at 40 km/h is 240 / 5 = 48 km/h.
question_forms: average speed for the whole journey

skills.name: Determine velocity as displacement over time, with direction
skills.mastery: The child tells velocity (displacement in a direction over time) from speed (distance over time), finds the displacement of a two-leg trip at right angles by Pythagoras, says a round trip has zero average velocity, and gives velocity with its direction: 30 km east then 40 km north in 2 h is 25 km/h.

prerequisites.reason: Displacement over two legs at right angles.

skills.name: Work out acceleration and deceleration
skills.mastery: The child finds acceleration as change in velocity over time (from a table, a graph or a story), in m/s squared, uses the change between the two readings asked, changes km/h to m/s before using m/s squared, and finds the time to stop as speed over deceleration: 54 km/h = 15 m/s, at 3 m/s squared it stops in 5 s.

prerequisites.reason: Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph.

skills.name: Find distance as the area under a velocity-time graph
skills.mastery: The child splits the area under a velocity-time graph into a triangle (speeding up from rest) and a rectangle (constant velocity) and adds them: up to 12 m/s in 6 s, then 12 m/s to 20 s, is 36 + 168 = 204 m.
question_forms: how far in the first 20 s

prerequisites.reason: Area of a triangle and a rectangle together.

skills.name: Identify longitudes on the globe
skills.mastery: The child describes longitudes as half-circles from the North Pole to the South Pole, measured in degrees east or west of the Greenwich meridian (0 degrees) up to 180 degrees, and gives the longitude of a place with E or W (Nairobi about 37 degrees E, Lima about 77 degrees W).

prerequisites.reason: Positions given by numbers from a zero line.
Angles measured in degrees round the Earth's axis.

skills.name: Relate a difference in longitude to a difference in time
skills.mastery: The child finds the difference in longitude (subtract when both are east or both west, add when on opposite sides of 0 degrees) and turns it into time at 4 minutes a degree (15 degrees an hour), and works back from a time difference to a longitude: 2 h 20 min = 140 minutes = 35 degrees.

prerequisites.reason: A difference across zero adds the two sides.

skills.name: Determine the local time of places on different longitudes
skills.mastery: The child finds the time difference from the longitudes, adds it for a place to the east (ahead) and takes it away for a place to the west (behind), keeps the leftover minutes, and for a flight adds the flight time first and then changes to the local time at the arrival city.
question_forms: what time does the plane land

prerequisites.reason: The time difference from the longitudes.
Adding a duration to a clock time.

skills.name: Approximate quantities by rounding before calculating
skills.mastery: The child rounds each number by its own digit (to the nearest ten, or to 1 significant figure) before working out, gives the estimate as the answer, and uses it to check an exact answer: 47.3 x 62.6 is about 50 x 60 = 3,000.

skills.name: Determine the error between an estimate and an actual measurement
skills.mastery: The child finds the error as the difference between the estimate (or measured value) and the actual value, always positive, and says whether the estimate was too big or too small: estimate 12,000, exact 11,280, error 720.

skills.name: Find the greatest possible error of a measurement
skills.mastery: The child says a reading to the nearest unit of the measuring step can be out by at most half that step (to the nearest 10 m: 5 m), whatever the size of the reading.
question_forms: how far out can it be

skills.name: Find the smallest and largest possible values of a measurement and of an area
skills.mastery: The child gives the lower and upper bounds of a measurement (reading minus and plus half the step: 12 m to the nearest metre lies from 11.5 m to 12.5 m), and finds the greatest possible area by multiplying the two upper bounds.

skills.name: Determine percentage error using actual measurements
skills.mastery: The child finds percentage error as error over the actual value times 100 (a bag of 80 kg estimated at 84 kg: 4 / 80 x 100 = 5%), and compares two measurements by their percentage errors, not by the size of the error alone or its unit.

sub_strands.design_notes: Official outcomes a to e are tested; f (promote the use) is not a question. Similar figures have equal angles and sides in one ratio (a), drawing similar figures (b), properties of enlargement, its centre and scale factor (c), drawing objects and images (d), and the linear scale factor (e), with area and volume factors as its square and cube. Five existing families use area and volume scale factors; KICD's outcome e names only the linear scale factor, so a teacher should confirm that area and volume factors belong in Grade 9. Drawing similar figures (b) and enlargements (d) have no family: a typed answer cannot check a drawing. similar-cartons-table builds its wrong answers in code and is tied at family level.

skills.name: Identify similar figures and their properties
skills.mastery: The child says two figures are similar when their angles are equal and all their sides are in the same ratio (each side multiplied by one scale factor), checks this for rectangles and triangles, and knows that adding the same length to every side does not give a similar figure.

prerequisites.reason: A ratio scale multiplies every length.

skills.name: Find a missing side of similar figures
skills.mastery: The child matches the corresponding sides (shortest with shortest), finds the scale factor from one pair, and multiplies (small to large) or divides (large to small) the partner of the missing side; uses similar triangles of shadows to find a height.

skills.name: Draw figures similar to a given figure
skills.mastery: The child multiplies every side of a figure by the same scale factor and keeps every angle, drawing the new figure with a ruler and protractor (or on squared paper), and checks it with the ratio of two pairs of sides.

skills.name: Determine properties of an enlargement: centre and scale factor
skills.mastery: The child knows an enlargement from a centre multiplies the distance of each point from the centre by the scale factor (from the origin it multiplies the coordinates), finds the centre by joining object and image points and extending the lines, and combines an enlargement with a translation in order.

skills.name: Draw the image of an object under an enlargement
skills.mastery: The child draws lines from the centre through each vertex, measures each distance from the centre, multiplies it by the scale factor along the same line, and joins the image points; the image is similar to the object.

skills.name: Determine the linear scale factor of similar figures
skills.mastery: The child finds the linear scale factor as a length on the image over the matching length on the object (large over small for an enlargement), and uses it the right way: multiply to go from small to large.

skills.name: Use the area and volume scale factors of similar figures
skills.mastery: The child uses the square of the linear scale factor for areas and its cube for volumes and capacities (a tank twice as wide holds 8 times as much), and works back from a volume factor to the linear factor by the cube root and on to the area factor by squaring.

prerequisites.reason: The cube root of a volume factor.

skills.name: Identify the sides of a right-angled triangle from a given angle
skills.mastery: The child names the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle, the longest side), the opposite side (across from the given angle) and the adjacent side (next to the given angle, not the hypotenuse), and renames them when the other acute angle is used.

prerequisites.reason: The hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle (Grade 7).

skills.name: Identify sine, cosine and tangent as ratios of sides
skills.mastery: The child writes sin = opposite / hypotenuse, cos = adjacent / hypotenuse and tan = opposite / adjacent for a given angle, picks the right fraction from a triangle with known sides, and uses the ratio to set up the side asked: opposite = hypotenuse x sin.

prerequisites.reason: A ratio written as a fraction.

skills.name: Read tables of trigonometric ratios for acute angles, both ways
skills.mastery: The child reads sin, cos or tan of an angle from the right column and row of the table, uses it to find a side (multiplying by the hypotenuse for the rise and run of a path), and reads the table backwards to find the angle whose ratio is given.

prerequisites.reason: Reading a mathematical table by row and column.

skills.name: Determine trigonometric ratios and angles using a calculator
skills.mastery: The child sets the calculator to degrees, keys sin, cos or tan then the angle, uses the inverse key (sin to the -1) to find an angle from a ratio, rounds to the accuracy asked, and checks against a known value (sin 30 = 0.5, tan 45 = 1).

prerequisites.reason: Knowing what the ratio values look like.

skills.name: Apply trigonometric ratios to find lengths in real situations
skills.mastery: The child sketches the right-angled triangle, marks the known and wanted sides from the angle, chooses the one ratio that joins them, rearranges (multiply when the unknown is on top, divide when it is underneath), and adds an eye height when an angle of elevation is measured from the eye: 40 m away at 35 degrees with the eye 1.5 m up gives 40 x 0.7002 + 1.5 = 29.5 m.

prerequisites.reason: Angles of elevation and eye height.

skills.name: Apply trigonometric ratios to find angles in real situations
skills.mastery: The child writes the ratio of the two known sides for the angle (a ramp rising 1.2 m over 5 m: tan x = 0.24), then finds the angle from the table or the inverse key (13.5 degrees), and checks the angle is sensible.

skills.name: Determine a suitable class width for grouping data
skills.mastery: The child finds the range (largest minus smallest), chooses a class width that gives about 5 to 10 classes (a range of 47 with width 10 gives 5 classes), and writes the class limits so that every value fits in exactly one class.

prerequisites.reason: Dividing the range by a width.

skills.name: Draw a frequency distribution table of grouped data
skills.mastery: The child tallies each value into its class (a value on a boundary into the higher class, as agreed), totals the frequencies, and checks that the total equals the number of values.

skills.name: Identify the modal class of grouped data
skills.mastery: The child picks the class with the highest frequency (the tallest bar), not the class with the highest values, and compares it with the next highest class by subtraction when asked how many more.
question_forms: how many more in the modal class

skills.name: Calculate the mean of grouped data using midpoints
skills.mastery: The child finds each class midpoint (halfway between its limits), multiplies by the frequency, adds the products, and divides by the total frequency (not by the number of classes): sum of fx 1,240 over 40 sacks is 31 kg.

skills.name: Determine the median of grouped data by interpolation
skills.mastery: The child finds the total frequency and the position n/2, adds frequencies until the class that holds it (the median class), counts those below it, and moves into the class in proportion: median = lower limit + ((n/2 - frequency below) / class frequency) x class width.

prerequisites.reason: Moving along a class in proportion.

skills.name: Read a cumulative frequency graph of grouped data
skills.mastery: The child reads "how many under a value" straight from a cumulative frequency graph and finds how many lie between two values by subtracting the two readings: under 40 minus under 20.

skills.name: Perform experiments with equally likely outcomes and list them
skills.mastery: The child lists all the equally likely outcomes of a fair coin, die or spinner (a die has 6), finds the probability of an event as favourable outcomes over all outcomes (an even number on a die: 3/6), and knows a spinner with unequal sectors does not give equally likely outcomes.

skills.name: Determine the range of probability and expected numbers
skills.mastery: The child places probabilities from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), compares likelihoods as fractions of the whole (red out of all beads, not the number of reds), and finds an expected number as probability times the number of trials (0.85 of 200 seeds is about 170).

skills.name: Identify mutually exclusive events in real life
skills.mastery: The child says two events are mutually exclusive when they cannot happen together (taking road A or road B on one trip), and not when they can overlap (playing football and playing netball), and explains why adding probabilities fails when there is an overlap.

skills.name: Find probabilities of mutually exclusive events by adding
skills.mastery: The child adds the probabilities of mutually exclusive events for "either A or B" (a raffle ticket winning a radio or a bag: 3/200 + 7/200 = 0.05) and finds "neither" as 1 minus that sum.

prerequisites.reason: Checking the events cannot both happen.

skills.name: Perform experiments involving independent events and multiply probabilities
skills.mastery: The child says two events are independent when one does not change the chance of the other (a coin and a spinner, the bus on Monday and on Tuesday), multiplies for "A and B" (0.5 x 1/6 = 1/12), and finds expected winners as probability times players.

skills.name: Find probabilities with and without replacement
skills.mastery: The child keeps the same chances on the second draw when the first is put back (with replacement: (3/8) x (3/8)), and reduces both the favourable count and the total by one when it is not put back ((3/8) x (2/7)), and explains why.

skills.name: Draw and use a tree diagram for two stages
skills.mastery: The child draws a tree with the outcomes of each stage on branches, writes each branch probability (changed on the second stage without replacement), multiplies along a path, and adds the paths that make the event ("exactly one grows" is two paths).

prerequisites.reason: Adding paths that cannot both happen.
